first.rationale: The competitor's entry pricing creates strong pull toward promotional_pricing, but memory_73 explicitly records that this lifts acquisition/revenue while materially degrading 30-day retention and warns against generalizing it. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is the wrong lever even though it is the most directly responsive one; matching a competitor on price would also likely anchor the price-sensitive segment we least want to over-serve. The two internal metrics that actually moved (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the funnel itself, and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a single onboarding intervention has the best chance of moving both. memory_86 (shortened onboarding lifts completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer signup fields lifts first-week activation) are mutually reinforcing evidence for that direction; memory_91 (in-product activation messaging) is the close alternative, so I am spending both verification pulls on memory_86 and memory_91 to (a) confirm memory_86's effect is real and not an artifact now 24 days stale, and (b) check whether memory_91's week-one engagement lift was measured on accounts that had already completed onboarding, which would make it a poor fix for an upstream completion drop. referral_incentive (memory_57) is sound but targets established customers and does nothing for the observed decline; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a different segment from the one under attack. Downstream risk flagged: stripping signup fields can reduce qualification/enrichment data and quietly shift the mix toward lower-quality accounts, so revenue quality, not just activation counts, must be in the readout. Running as a standard_experiment with a holdout rather than a broad rollout, since the inherited results predate the current competitive environment and the segment mix may have shifted. If verification shows memory_86's lift was small or segment-specific, I will fall back to activation_messaging rather than to pricing.
